title: Black Hat USA 2025 Keynote | Chronicles of Counter-Intelligence from the Citizen Lab

segments.text: Please welcome to the stage the founder of Black Hat, Jeff Moss.
Hello. Good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for making it to our afternoon session.
I've just got a couple of thoughts as I introduce, before I introduce Ron DeBert.
Let me see, by a show of hands here, who here would sort of, if
you had to put a label on yourself, would you consider yourself civil society? Yay,
civil society. Okay. I would put myself, and
I'd definitely put Ron firmly in the camp of civil society. And I think that's
because when I started DEF CON and I moved away from my
days of Ernst & Young, I realized
the power of community, but also I'm a small business guy, small to medium. I
don't have billion dollar budgets. I don't have tons of resources. But what I do
have is I have friends and I have ideals. And when I
ended up at the chief security officer at ICANN, clearly pretty much it's
a nonprofit, public benefit corporation, but it was really civil society.
And through there, I could really see how the people were building the internet, the
infrastructure, the protocols. Yes, there was some business there,
but not really. All those core protocols, open source software, civil society, thank you very
much. You're building your products on civil society software, essentially. And
so I am a big fan of trying to support and promote any civil society
involvement because it ends up being sort of the seeds that grow into big companies.
The thing that's changing now though, I think, in the last six months is with
the federal government stepping back. Who steps forward? Who fills
the vacuum? And I believe part of it unfortunately, are going to be the
hyperscalers. The Googles, Microsoft, Amazon, those types of companies. They have to step forward. If
they're trying to protect their customers and they're getting less help from the federal government,
they're just going to have to do more. Which means the hyperscalers will
centralize their importance more. We will rely on
them more. I think that that
level of centralization without a counterbalance could be problematic. So that's why
I'm so interested in hearing the perspective from Ron from civil society. He's at the
Monk School. I've known Ron since my ICANN days. He
spends a lot of time from the civil society side figuring out what nation
states are doing that they probably shouldn't be doing, what criminals are doing, What activists
are being targeted? How are they being targeted? How can you counter it? And I
really think in this current kind of chaotic time we're in, we really need to
listen to the voices of those people who have been in the trenches for years
from a civil society perspective because they can kind of give us a crystal ball
of what we can expect. So with that, I'm really proud and honored to introduce
Ron Deaver.
Well, thank you, Jeff, for that introduction, and thank you, everybody. It's a real honor
to be here at Black Hat. Thank you for coming, and I appreciate all the
work that everyone does. So if you know nothing else about the Citizen Lab, you
probably have heard about our investigations into NSO groups, Pegasus spyware. Over the
last 10-plus years, we've produced dozens of reports based on
investigations into the abuse of mercenary spyware. In just about
every region of the world, companies selling this technology to governments, which they've used to
hack into the phones of journalists, human rights defenders, anti-corruption advocates,
lawyers and family members and so on. Probably the most famous of our
investigations began with this guy. His name is Omar Abdulaziz. He was a Saudi.
He moved to Canada to study at university, became involved in digital activism.
Back in 2018, we discovered that his phone was hacked with Pegasus spyware.
Omar was a friend of Jamal Khashoggi, the Washington Post journalist. And they had been
communicating for many, many months over what they thought was secure, end-to-end, encrypted
application, WhatsApp. What they didn't realize was that the whole time, Saudi operatives
were eavesdropping on those conversations. In fact, I think if you look at those exchanges,
you could see they had a slight degree of paranoia about them as this was
going on. We published our report about the hacking into Omar's device on
October 1st. The very next day, Jamal Khashoggi went into
the Saudi consulate in Istanbul and was met by a
15-member hit squad who murdered him and dismembered him. Now, if you speak
to people in the industry, they say, hey, we sell this technology, it's very strictly
controlled to help governments investigate serious matters of crime and terrorism.
If you're a criminal, don't be afraid. Well, the main takeaway of the Citizen Lab's
research over the last 20 years or so is actually you should be very
afraid. A bit more about the Citizen Lab for those of you who don't know.
We are not a company. We don't have a booth in the business hall. I'm
not here to sell you anything. We're not even an NGO. We're an academic research
lab based at the University of Toronto, where I'm a full professor. I'm the principal
investigator of the Citizen Lab, and I founded it in 2001. And in fact, we
probably do work very similar to a lot of people in this room. We use
interdisciplinary approaches, a lot of forensic science, to do what we do, the main
difference is the focus of our research. We see ourselves as filling a kind of
gap. We focus on cybersecurity issues that arise out of human rights
concerns. When I founded the lab, I had this vision that we would do
counterintelligence for civil society, and fast forward to today, and I guess the old
adage comes to mind, careful what you wish for. You may not remember that
we were part of the team that produced arguably the very first public cyber espionage
report ever. Way back in 2009, it was called the Tracking Ghost Net Report.
And in that investigation, we found that the computers of the Office of the Dalai
Lama and dozens of high value targets around the world had been compromised
by Chinese threat actors. And almost as an afterthought, we decided, hey, we should give
the threat actors a name. And so we came up with this name, GhostNet. And
afterwards, of course, there was this proliferation of threat intelligence reports and all of these
different cute names for APT actors. So if you're one of those people that's really
annoyed by the nomenclature, I think you can blame us for a bit of that.
Citizen Lab has been behind Many firsts when it comes to investigations in mercenary spyware.
Going back to 2011, 2012, we uncovered the abuse of products
from companies like Gamma Group, Hacking Team, NSO Group, all the way up to Paragon,
which is currently in our radar and I'll talk about in a few minutes. I'd
like to go through a couple of our greatest hits, our most memorable cases, and
this is certainly One of them ranks up very highly. This is Ahmad Mansour. He's
a human rights defender based in the UAE. And back in 2016, he received these
two text messages purporting to show evidence of torture in Emirati prisons, something
that would tempt him to click on those links. But he was suspicious, and he
decided instead he would forward them to Bill Marzak, who's right here in the front
row, actually. Bill Marzak is our lead technical researcher at the Citizen Lab, the
architect of a lot of our research. And Bill appropriated an iPhone from an office
mate and infected his device in the laboratory setting, and he captured Pegasus
spyware and the zero-day exploit chain. It was the first time anybody had come across
NSO Group in the wild. And we did a responsible disclosure to Apple. They issued
an emergency security patch, I think within about 11 days of Ahmad Mansour
sending us those text messages. And that was the first time we've done responsible disclosures
to Apple. We've done them many times since, as well as other companies. Speaking of
responsible disclosures, I'd say this was a very important one as well back in 2021
when we discovered another Pegasus zero day, in this case a zero
click, which we called forced entry, we discovered that from the infected phone
of a Saudi activist. And that Saudi activist is named Lujain Al-Hatul.
She's an activist in Saudi Arabia who had been advocating for a woman's right
to drive a car in Saudi Arabia without a chaperone. That's Saudi Arabia's idea
of a criminal or a terrorist. Once again, we did a responsible disclosure to
Apple. And remarkably, this time, Apple did a whole bunch of things that
surprised us and made us quite happy. They introduced these new features, Lockdown Mode, to
better protect high-risk users. They sued NSO Group and later withdrew the suit,
but they also announced a $10 million contribution to support cyber security
research of the sort that Citizen Lab engages in, which is very important. That went
to a third party fund. Citizen Lab, like many other groups in this space, cannot
accept money from corporations or governments. And they also started sending out these threat
notifications notifications whenever they discover one of their customers phones has been
hacked, they send these out. And this is doing enormous triage for groups like ours.
They essentially shake a tree and victims fall to the ground and make their way
to us. So this has been a really important development. And it's going on up
until today. So another example of these notifications has to
do with yet another mercenary spyware firm, in this case called Paragon.
Paragon has advertised itself as kind of the clean NSO group, a
responsible mercenary spyware vendor. Well, we discovered that they had a
zero-click exploit that was targeting WhatsApp groups, and so we
notified WhatsApp, and they patched the exploit, and then sent out notifications of their
own, and we discovered that the Italian government was using Paragon spyware to
hack the phones of migrant support workers, and then Apple sent out notifications,
and we discovered that Italian government was using Paragon to hack into the phones of
journalists as well. We've had some pretty big blockbuster country
cases. One of the most important in my mind was a series of reports we
did on the abuse of mercenary spyware in Mexico, just a tsunami of
abuse cases. The Mexican government or agencies within Mexico had been
using Pegasus spyware to hack the phones of regime critics,
anti-corruption advocates, journalists, political opposition, human rights defenders,
on and on and on. It was really quite a shocking, appalling example of the
way in which this technology could be abused. And we had quite a year. We
had four front page New York Times exclusives in one year focusing on our research
reports. And by the way, those were co-authored by Nicole Pearlroth, who's also giving a
keynote here tomorrow. I highly recommend going to see what she has to say. Now,
you think all of that publicity would bring about some kind of change. Well, after
we reported yet another case of abuse, former President AMLO simply said,
oh, that stuff is all made up. And we've subsequently learned through court discovery proceedings
that another former president of Mexico, Nieto, had been bribed $25
million by NSO Group's middlemen in order to further contracts in that country.
So some pretty sordid stuff there. Another big country case, In
2022, we unearthed a massive domestic cyber espionage operation in
Spain, targeting a huge cross-section of Catalan civil society, including the
sitting president of Catalonia had his phone hacked with Pegasus. Shortly after our report
was published, the head of intelligence was sacked because of our report. And there you
can see myself and Elias Campo, a Citizen Lab researcher, worked on that investigation
when that happened, holding up the front pages of Spanish newspapers. Shortly afterwards, something
very similar happened in Greece. The head of intelligence quit there after
our reporting showed that the Greek government was using yet another type of mercenary spyware,
Predator, to hack the phones of journalists and political opposition figures. So we've made a
lot of enemies in high places who don't like the work that we do. Speaking
of those type of people, a really interesting case is when Bill Marzak discovered
that Sheikh Mohammed, the Prime Minister of the UAE, had actually used Pegasus spyware
to hack into the phone of his ex-wife, Princess Haya, with whom he was
embroiled in a child custody dispute in UK courts. But he didn't just hack
her phone. He hacked her security detail as well and hacked the phone of his
lawyer, Baroness Shackleton, who's a sitting member of the UK House of Lords.
And among her other clients at the time were then Prince Charles and Paul McCartney.
So you can imagine the ripples that went through UK society when this was disclosed.
But things really took a Fellini-esque turn later during court proceedings when Sherry
Blair, the wife of former British Prime Minister Tony Blair,
disclosed in her court testimony that shortly after Bill Marzak confidentially
and privately disclosed his findings to Baroness Shackleton, she was
contacted by NSO Group, which was one of the clients for her PR firm, to
do so as well. And the question is, well, how did they know what we
had confidentially disclosed? Around the same time, we
discovered a device in 10 Downing Street was hacked with Pegasus. And it could very
well have been Boris Johnson's phone. And I do recall when we did the responsible
disclosure to UK authorities, they said something like, oh no, not again.
We've had some great victories. One of the most important was in spring
2023, President Biden signed an executive order
prohibiting 18 federal agencies, intelligence agencies, from procuring
spyware from firms like NSO Group. And there you can see myself and John
Scott Railton, who leads our targeted threats team at the White House, briefing the National
Security Council leading up to that executive order. JSR is a wonderful person. I'm
guessing Many people in this room at one point or another have interacted with
JSR at some point in time. And speaking personally as a political scientist, to have
a president of the United States sign an executive order on an issue you care
about is a pretty big deal. It's like winning the holy grail. There's
lots of litigation around the work that we do. Victims suing companies like NSO
Group or suing governments that have hacked into their phones or companies like WhatsApp
suing mercenary spyware firms. Generally speaking, this is a very good thing.
You want a pathway to justice for victims. But as we found out, there's lots
of risks even if you're not a party to that litigation. We found this out
during the WhatsApp versus NSO group litigation when NSO group tried
to use the discovery proceedings to find out as much as they could about how
we go about fingerprinting their infections. And fortunately for us, the judge kept
swatting them down. But we had to arm up with legal counsel support. And let
me tell you, that costs a lot of money to defend yourself. We've been sued,
we've been threatened with lawsuits many times. One of the most memorable for me was
back in 2018, we were researching the abuse of Sandvine's deep packet
inspection systems, which we discovered was being used to facilitate the injection of
malware into targets devices. And as part of that investigation, Bill purchased
a secondhand Sandvine deep packet inspection device. And when it was
delivered to us, I think the credentials were taped on the top right there, making
it very convenient for us to experiment with it, develop a fingerprint so we could
scan the internet and understand better how Sandvines DPI systems work. Well,
in anticipation of that publication, as is customary, we sent Sandvines a letter asking if
they had any comment. And they sent a letter back, not just to me, but
to just about everybody at the University of Toronto, where we're based, threatening to sue
us if we published our report and demanding that we give back the packet logic
device. And fortunately, the University of Toronto's lawyers said, hell no, that's our
device, we're keeping it. We went ahead with publication. But it was kind of scary
for a few weeks there while we were going through that process. A couple years
later we found out that they were still up to it, involved in
injecting malware into a device of an Egyptian politician's phone. And
after that report came out, the Sandvine was placed on a
US sanctions list. And that really hurt the company. They started laying off people. Eventually
they went, bankrupt altogether and rebranded entirely with a new human rights
philosophy, which goes to show that revenge is a dish best
served as an evidence-based research report, at least from my perspective.
Thank you. Now, as you might guess, there's a lot of
pushback. When you do the type of work that we do, we
face a lot of disinformation, for example. Here's just one example. This was a graphic
that ran on Polish prime time state television. And I was shocked to see
that there I am in the middle of a mob diagram with reporting lines to
Julian Assange and Russian intelligence. Never met Julian Assange. certainly not a
pawn of Russian intelligence. In fact, we've published many reports on Russian cyber espionage.
Ironically, last year we published a report on Russian hacking,
and afterwards the Kremlin put the school in which the Citizen Lab is located
designated us an undesirable organization. So if you're going to smear us, at
least Google us first, because that was really not credible at all. More seriously,
at one point in 2019, several of my staff members were targeted in a covert
private intelligence operation by a company called Black Cube, made up of
ex-Massad agents. They tried to secretly gather recordings of
my staff that would be meant to incriminate us in some way. But JSR, who
is one of the targets, got together with Raphael Satter, who was then working for
Associated Press, and we organized a sting in a Manhattan restaurant and exposed the agent.
So if you Google that, yeah, you get to see all of him panicking, and
he's now out of work, let me tell you. With all that going on, people
ask me a lot, what keeps you awake at night? Well actually I sleep very
well at night because I feel like I have the best job in the world
and I'm very lucky to wake up and work with so many talented people. But
I do have some concerns. And this is a graphic I've been playing with.
I like to call this welcome to my nightmare. Or another way of looking at
this, to borrow a phrase from my friend Cory Doctorow, this is the inshittification
of the human condition. I believe that we're locked in this vicious cycle
right now. By the way, self-reinforcing feedback loops like this are quite
common in human societies. And unfortunately, they can have negative feedback loops. And there could
be several interlocking social forces that come together. And these can be disastrous. I mean,
sometimes you can reform your way out of them, but just as often they lead
to some type of catastrophe or collapse. And I really do believe that we're in
the midst of this right now, and I'd like to unpack it for you a
bit, beginning with the upper quadrant, the properties of the digital ecosystem, and
especially social media and surveillance capitalism, which everyone in this room
will be familiar with. So just to remind you, to get us all on the
same page, every application that exists on the internet, virtually every
application in social media for sure, has a higher and a lower level function. The
lower level function is the advertised one. A bike sharing app, a flight
check-in app, any hotel app, whatever it is, that's the lower level function. The higher
level function is to gather as much information from us, their customers, as possible.
Our social relationships, our habits, our personal tastes, our biometric
features, in order to push advertisements in our direction. That's surveillance capitalism
at work. So no matter how much the platforms advertise
as putting information at our fingertips and help us navigate the world around us,
it's important to remember that we're ultimately the livestock for their data farms. And yes,
once you see that, you can't unsee it. Simple stuff.
Why Amazon wants an AI bracelet that records everything you say? Why? That's a rhetorical
question, I think. It's this kind of relentless logic to get closer and closer,
invasive by design, more approximate to the person in order to gather as much
information as you can. And this is getting, of course, right down logically to the
physiological elements of our personalities, our retinal
movements, our dilation of the pupils, our cheeks being flustered.
What content excites us in order to get us when we're most vulnerable? Human
nature being what it is, unfortunately we're attracted to content that is emotional, that is
conspiratorial, that makes us angry, that makes us outraged.
No surprise, that's why most social media platforms are now a toxic mess. X
being of course the most obvious example with the new Grok Companions designed to
shock and entertain users. That's the business model of surveillance capitalism at work.
Now if you just take those properties which I would put under the umbrella of
algorithmic rage farming, it turns out if you were to be in a laboratory
setting and you tried to create in a petri dish the conditions that would be
perfect for professionalized disinformation,
privatized subversion, dark PR, you couldn't do better than what exists right
now. And not surprisingly, we're seeing stories like this now flooding
the news disinformation is becoming just inescapable now,
and it's no surprise because of the properties of the digital ecosystem. Some of this
is very crude, easy to spot, but obviously it's going to get more and more
sophisticated, especially as private companies get into the mix, offering dark PR
services designed to credit, discredit adversaries. We got a little
taste of this professional industry back in 2016 with this company, Cy Group.
Reportedly, George Nader, a convicted pedophile and
Trump supporter, was trying at the time to broker a deal between Gulf states who
wanted to support Trump and this company, Cy Group. They've since gone insolvent, but what
struck me about this company was their tagline, Reality is a Matter of Perception. It's
kind of like Jean Baudrillard meets the Mossad. Now, if you fast forward to today,
you have examples like this, Team Jorge exposed by undercover
investigation bragging about covert involvement in 33 presidential elections. I have
no doubt that sort of thing is going on and a lot better than this
operation, which is probably very sloppy for them to get caught. Now there are other
elements of the digital ecosystem that are also propelling forward this mercenary
surveillance and commercial information operations. Obviously the invasive by
design features are very important here to the proliferation of spyware firms and
location tracking firms. We all carry around these devices now with
us all the time. We go to bed with them. We have several devices, wearable
devices. Our lives are entrusted to these devices, and that's
propelled forward an industry that the Citizen Lab has tracked, whose purpose is to
hack inside those devices. And as we have shown in our research, because the industry
is so poorly regulated, we're seeing a tsunami of abuses worldwide. And generally
speaking, this is an industry, my observation is highly, highly
unethical. I also believe that this industry is
premised on furthering a kind of collective insecurity. When most of you
find vulnerabilities, you don't harbor them. Maybe you do,
I don't know, but I'm hoping most of you do responsible disclosures. These companies obviously
don't do that, and the exploits are getting quite sophisticated. Zero click versions of
exploits where you can simply take over any phone anywhere in the world. And the
capabilities, when you look at them, are really profound. And to me, I can
understand why this business is so lucrative. If you put yourself in the position of
a government spy and you have these capabilities, it's almost godlike.
You get inside an adversary's life highly intoxicating. It must be very addictive to
have that. But even if you don't contract with a mercenary spyware firm, There are
many other ways to skin a cat, and the one that interests me today is
advertising intelligence, or ADINT, where you have these mercenary surveillance firms that have figured out
that they can exploit data brokerage marketplaces and take advantage of the
fact that there are all these advertising and Bluetooth beacons out there and sensors in
buildings like this one that track our movements mostly for commercial purposes. So you have
these companies that are basically operating in crossover markets,
like this one, Aspectum, which markets foot traffic data, very reasonable. I
looked at some of their use cases, disaster and wildfires mapping, okay. But then I
noticed, what the heck is this? Social unrest monitoring, uh-oh. And then they also have
a map showing how their technology could be used to track Black Lives Matters protests.
That's very ominous in light of what's going on today. Here's a firm that's much
more just straightforward about it, Patterns, another Israeli firm. As they say,
people always have their phones with them, especially during crises. They claim to have over
5 billion unique user IDs profiled. And they advertise being able to,
say, draw a geofence around a room like this and spit out detailed intelligence
dossiers on everyone in the room based on this type of advertising intelligence, things like
your home address, work location, device details, and so much more. Scary stuff.
Here's another ad-in firm, Fogg, whose Reveal portal advertises the ability to
identify smart devices' beddowns. I guess that means your
home or other locations of interest. Creepy. And of course, all of this runs
through the telecommunications infrastructure, at the heart of which are some very serious
vulnerabilities having to do with the signaling protocols that are used, usually go under the
rubric of SS7. So mercenary surveillance firms like Raison have
realized that if they can lease global title to operate as a telco, they can
get inside these signaling networks and use it to track people's location relative
to the nearest cell tower or intercept SMS messages that are used for two-factor authentication
or even in some cases downgrade the call in order to intercept the call itself.
This is one such firm that operates in this space called Ability and they get
the award for the creepiest slogan, while others talk, we listen. No
thanks. Now we thought at the Citizen Lab that it would be difficult to undertake
investigations, evidence-based investigations of these SS7 vendors because unlike
spyware firms, they don't leave traces on the device that would enable forensic research.
But Bill discovered in one case involving a company called Circles that operates in this
space, that they had misconfigured their checkpoint firewalls and he used that
signature to scan the entire internet back in 2020 to map out their
government clients. And as you can see here, it's basically a rogues gallery of autocrats
and human rights abusing countries. Again, that's
2020. Imagine what the customer base for companies like that look like now.
Gary Miller, who is a whistleblower from this industry, has come to work at the
Citizen Lab, and he brought with him data that shows Saudi Arabia
undertook millions of secret tracking requests of the sort I'm talking about
over a four month period following Saudi users as they are roaming throughout the United
States. Need I remind you, this is a government that engages in targeted assassinations.
Now, what is this all doing to civil society? Getting back to Jeff's opening comments.
Well, 25 years ago, 30 years ago, when I started studying this area, everyone
had great enthusiasm about the technology. They were saying that it's going to lead to
massive people power and new forms of democratization. What we're seeing
is exactly the opposite. We're seeing civil society under assault, major chilling
effects, paranoia, fear, withdrawal. This is Karine Kanimba.
She's a Rwandan who's now a US citizen. Her father, who managed Hotel
Rwanda in Rwanda, he was kidnapped and rendered back to
Rwanda, and while she was advocating for her father's release, we discovered her phone was
hacked with Pegasus spyware, and you can see her remarks here are pretty representative of
the type of emotions, the psychological trauma that victims experience,
that we interact with by the dozens. And this type of transnational repression
is spreading. Even if the governments are not able to tap into this sophisticated mercenary
spyware marketplace, they have homegrown methods to accomplish the same things. And we're
seeing state repression moving beyond national borders, attacking
activists, some of them even contracting out to organize criminals in order to finish the
job. Now, what this is doing finally is helping
to spread authoritarian practices worldwide. Let me give you some
examples. So this is Freedom House's indices, their democratic
rankings. They say that their scores show 19 years of decline
in global freedom. 19 years. That's back to 2006 when Twitter
was launched, when Google purchased YouTube, when
Facebook started its news feed. I'm not a big fan of monocausal explanations for anything,
but that's a pretty strong correlation for my vicious cycle right there. And
then there's this, which keeps me awake at night. It's more than symbolic that these
two have become buddies. Nayib Bukele, the self-described
world's coolest dictator, who just last week had Congress in El
Salvador eliminate term limits. And then you have Donald Trump, dictator, oh, but only for
one day, who is now mooting eliminating term limits and running again for the
presidency. Look at the gold in that picture. I mean, this says it all.
Honestly, people, we're in a crisis right now. I'm a political scientist. I've
studied authoritarianism my entire life. What's going on in your country right now, I'm a
Canadian, I'm here to say this to you, checks all the boxes of authoritarian
decline. And what really worries me right now is what's happening with the tech industry
and these trends in the United States with basically tech leaders falling into line, getting
on the bus, going to Saudi Arabia to investment summits to try to get money
for what they're doing. despite the fact that this is a person that's gone around
murdering journalists and imprisoning and torturing people like Lujain Al-Hatul. And at
the center of it all is Palantir. CEO Alex Karp has published a book called
The Technological Republic, which basically makes the case that Silicon Valley should
get on board the U.S. war-making machine. Of course, it's a self-interested argument.
His stock is basically ballooned. since Trump was elected. And there's some very
controversial things they're now involved in, including building a surveillance platform to help with this
mass deportation regime. Help this person who's described what they're doing in
horribly frightening terms. Amazon-like mass deportation
system, prime but with human beings. Let me tell you, that doesn't give me any
confidence. And remember that, Doge has gone through and collected all of this
personal data that's being fed into this massive surveillance dragnet.
This is a platform that's put together by a collective called Lockdown Systems. They're trying
to collectively determine how many people are being detained and they have close to
50,000 people. Look at that figure, 71% without criminal records.
okay, this is happening with people that you maybe ignore, marginalized people, displaced people,
people working in this hotel room. But you gotta ask yourself, who's next?
And the administration is now purchasing up all of the technology that I just
described. using AI to undertake social media surveillance of immigrants, refugees,
visitors to this country like me. But they also want to know if you're posting
negative things about them online. And they're contracting with companies like this, Cobwebs,
which, no surprise, founded by veterans of IDF special
units. When companies like this contract with the United States, it's
basically a good housekeeping seal of approval for them. And it will help
proliferate the mercenary surveillance industry outside of the United States. Not
surprisingly, NSO Group is furiously lobbying right now, trying to reverse that
executive order. And we're not just seeing passive surveillance collection, You should
fully expect there to be influence operations undertaken at a domestic level in
the United States. We can see it happening already with AI powered undercover bot
for cops posing as a vaguely defined protester. Imagine if J. Edgar Hoover
had this type of capability. And of course, all of this is happening at a
time when the tech platforms are getting rid of their trust and safety teams, eliminating
fact checking. Oh, and X, you have its chat bot that's gone on a Nazi
meltdown, but that hasn't stopped X from signing a $200 million deal
with the Pentagon. And of course, X itself is simultaneously taking
steps quite aggressively to limit public interest researchers like my
organization from understanding what they're doing and being very litigious in the process.
And all of this is happening in the context of attacks on academic freedom and
universities, something that for a person like me is an existential risk. I
can tell you confidently, I'm 100% sure that something like the
Citizen Lab could not exist in the United States right now. and I'm not even
sure we'll be able to exist that much longer if these trends continue.
Which gets me back to my nightmare, my vicious cycle.
You know, I've been doing this for a long time and I've never been more
concerned about what's going on in the world, but I do have a call for
action for you. First though, I want to say a heartfelt thank you everybody
